subject: Science
name: Science, Year 7
placeName: Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory

points.title: Why scientists classify living things
points.brief: Grouping organisms by shared features makes the huge variety of life easier to identify, study and talk about.

points.title: The Linnaean hierarchy
points.brief: Living things are sorted into ever smaller groups, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, with each group sharing more features.

points.title: Scientific names
points.brief: Each species has a two-part Latin name, its genus then its species, such as Homo sapiens, so scientists everywhere name it the same way.

points.title: Using a dichotomous key
points.brief: A dichotomous key identifies an organism through a series of two-way choices about its features, each choice splitting the group in two.

points.title: First Nations Australians' classification systems
points.brief: First Nations Australians have long classified plants and animals by features such as use, habitat, season and relationships, which can differ from the Linnaean system.

points.title: Producers, consumers and decomposers
points.brief: Producers make their own food from sunlight, consumers eat other organisms, and decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

points.title: Food chains and food webs
points.brief: A food chain shows one feeding path, and the arrows point from the food to the eater. A food web joins many chains to show how an ecosystem's organisms depend on each other.

points.title: Energy flow in an ecosystem
points.brief: Energy enters as sunlight, passes from one feeding level to the next, and much of it is lost as heat at each step, so there are fewer organisms higher up a food web.

points.title: Biotic and abiotic factors
points.brief: Biotic factors are the living parts of an ecosystem, and abiotic factors are the non-living ones such as temperature, water, light and soil. Both affect population sizes.

points.title: Changes that disrupt ecosystems
points.brief: Removing a predator or pollinator, clearing habitat or bringing in a species such as the cane toad changes populations right through a food web.

points.title: Fire management by First Nations Australians
points.brief: For tens of thousands of years, First Nations Australians have used planned, cool burning to manage Country, which has shaped where plants and animals live.

points.title: Why we have seasons
points.brief: The Earth's axis is tilted, so through the year each hemisphere takes turns facing the sun more directly, getting more concentrated light and longer days in summer.

points.title: Phases of the moon
points.brief: The moon reflects sunlight. As it orbits the Earth about every 29.5 days, we see different amounts of its lit half, from new moon to full moon and back.

points.title: Solar and lunar eclipses
points.brief: A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth. A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth's shadow falls on the moon.

points.title: Tides
points.brief: The moon's gravity, and to a lesser extent the sun's, pulls on the oceans to make high and low tides. Spring tides come when the sun and moon line up.

points.title: First Nations Australians' knowledge of the sky
points.brief: First Nations Australians have used the moon's phases, the stars and seasonal signs in calendars to predict tides, seasons and when foods are ready.

points.title: What a force is
points.brief: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons with a force meter. A force arrow shows its size by its length and its direction by where it points.

points.title: Balanced and unbalanced forces
points.brief: Balanced forces cancel out, so an object stays still or keeps moving steadily. Unbalanced forces make it start, stop, speed up, slow down or change direction.

points.title: Mass and the effect of a force
points.brief: The same force changes the motion of a light object more than a heavy one, so a heavier object needs a bigger force to start or stop it.

points.title: Gravity, mass and weight
points.brief: Gravity is a pulling force between masses. Weight is the force of Earth's gravity on an object, so it depends on mass, while mass stays the same anywhere.

points.title: Simple machines
points.brief: Levers, pulleys and inclined planes change the size or direction of the force needed for a job, such as lifting a load with less effort.

chapters.title: Particle theory and states of matter

points.title: The particle theory of matter
points.brief: All matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving and attract each other, with space between them.

points.title: Solids, liquids and gases
points.brief: In a solid, particles are packed close and vibrate in place. In a liquid, they are close but slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and move freely, which is why gases can be squashed.

points.title: Changes of state
points.brief: Adding heat makes particles move faster and spread out, so substances melt and boil. Losing heat slows them, so substances condense and freeze.

points.title: Diffusion
points.brief: Particles spread from where there are many to where there are few, because they keep moving. Diffusion is faster in gases than in liquids, and faster when warmer.

points.title: Pure substances and mixtures
points.brief: A pure substance has only one kind of particle. A mixture has two or more substances mixed but not joined, so they can be separated by physical means.

points.title: Solutions, solutes and solvents
points.brief: In a solution, a solute such as salt dissolves into a solvent such as water and spreads out evenly. Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves so much.

points.title: Filtration and decanting
points.brief: Filtration catches undissolved solid particles in filter paper while the liquid passes through. Decanting pours a liquid off a solid that has settled.

points.title: Evaporation and crystallisation
points.brief: Heating a solution evaporates the solvent and leaves the dissolved solid behind. Slow evaporation lets larger crystals form.

points.title: Distillation and chromatography
points.brief: Distillation boils a liquid and condenses the vapour to collect it pure. Chromatography separates dissolved substances, such as dyes in ink, by how far they travel up paper.

points.title: Choosing a separation method
points.brief: The right method depends on the property that differs, such as particle size, density, solubility or boiling point, as in water treatment or First Nations Australians' yandying of seeds.

units.title: Science as a human endeavour and inquiry

points.title: How new evidence changes science
points.brief: Scientific ideas can change when new evidence or tools appear, as when better microscopes showed new groups of living things.

points.title: Culture and scientific knowledge
points.brief: People from different cultures, including First Nations Australians, have built knowledge of the natural world through long observation, and their views can shape what science studies.

points.title: Weighing a scientific solution
points.brief: A science-based response to a problem, such as bringing in a species for pest control, has to be judged on its ethical, environmental, social and economic effects.

points.title: Science communication
points.brief: How science is reported in news, ads and social media affects what people believe and what rules governments make, so it should be clear and based on evidence.

points.title: Questions, predictions and hypotheses
points.brief: An investigable question can be tested. A hypothesis is a testable idea that explains something, and a prediction says what will happen if it is right.

points.title: Independent, dependent and controlled variables
points.brief: In a fair test you change one variable, measure another, and keep every other variable the same, so any change can be put down to the one you changed.

points.title: Measuring with precision
points.brief: Choosing the right instrument and reading it carefully at eye level gives precise measurements, recorded with the correct units.

points.title: Tables and graphs
points.brief: Results go in a table with the independent variable first. A line graph suits continuous data and a column graph suits categories.

points.title: Patterns, trends and anomalies
points.brief: A trend is the general direction of the data. An anomaly is a result that does not fit the pattern, and it may come from an error.
